events.description: The video opens with a transcript credit showing the transcriber and reviewer, accompanied by an on‑screen note that the event is an independently organized TEDx event.
events.title: Opening credits and TEDx intro

events.description: Richard Stallman speaks on stage, stating that free software is the first battle for cyberspace liberation and asks who controls the computer.
events.title: Stallman introduces free software concept

events.description: He continues asking who really controls the computer, suggesting it could be a big company, and asks what a computer is.
events.title: Stallman questions computer control

events.description: Stallman explains that a computer is a universal machine that executes any computation given by a program, fetching and carrying out instructions.
events.title: Defining a computer as universal machine

events.description: He describes how a program provides instructions that the computer follows, enabling it to perform any task when the right program is written.
events.title: Programs give computers instructions

events.description: Stallman notes that although a computer seems to follow user commands, it may actually be executing instructions imposed by a company, limiting user control.
events.title: Stallman warns about hidden instruction sources

events.description: He explains that software either empowers users or subjugates them, with no middle ground.
events.title: Two possibilities: user control vs program control

events.description: He states that for users to control a program they must have the four essential freedoms, which are shown on screen.
events.title: Stallman introduces the four essential freedoms

events.description: Richard Stallman explains the four essential freedoms, distinguishes free software from gratis, and introduces the term Libre.
events.title: Defining free software

events.description: Stallman states that freedom zero is the right to run a program for any purpose.
events.title: Freedom zero explained

events.description: He defines freedom one as the ability to study and modify source code, then asks what source code is.
events.title: Freedom one introduced

events.description: Stallman describes source code as readable text and executable as unreadable numbers.
events.title: Source vs executable

events.description: He argues that without source code, studying and changing a program is extremely hard.
events.title: Need source to modify

events.description: Stallman says having source lets each user copy and modify software for personal use.
events.title: Individual control via source

events.description: He states that non‑programmers also need collective control to adapt software.
events.title: Collective control needed

events.description: Stallman explains that groups can collaborate, with programmers implementing changes for the group’s needs.
events.title: Group adaptation of software

events.description: Richard Stallman says others can use the software any way they wish, emphasizing the freedom to run it for any purpose.
events.title: Stallman explains freedom to use software

events.description: He explains that freedom two allows users to redistribute exact copies of the software, showing on‑screen text 'Freedom 2' and 'Redistribute it'.
events.title: Stallman defines Freedom 2: redistribute copies

events.description: He states freedom three lets users share modified copies, with on‑screen text 'Freedom 3', 'Redistribute' and 'with changes'.
events.title: Stallman defines Freedom 3: redistribute modified versions

events.description: The speaker explains that with all freedoms users control the software; lacking any freedom lets the program and developer control users.
events.title: Users control vs program controls

events.description: The speaker argues that non‑free software gives developers unjust power over users, labeling it proprietary and calling for its removal.
events.title: Proprietary software as unjust power

events.description: The speaker says proprietary software may spy on users, citing Amazon as an example shown on screen.
events.title: Proprietary software can snoop users

events.description: He notes proprietary software can snoop, track, restrict, and remotely delete books, laughing as he shows a 'FORBIDDEN' slide.
events.title: Stallman warns of software tracking and deletion

events.description: He cites Amazon deleting Orwell's book and Sony forcing PS3 upgrades that disable functionality, shown on screen.
events.title: Examples of harmful upgrades and deletions

events.description: Stallman explains that Sony can forcibly change software remotely, as illustrated by a PS3 warning screen.
events.title: Sony forced software change

events.description: Stallman says Microsoft can change Windows remotely and shares bugs with the NSA to attack users.
events.title: Microsoft back door and NSA

events.description: Stallman describes how proprietary software owners exploit power to insert malicious features, not out of sadism.
events.title: Proprietary software power abuse

events.description: Stallman says companies exploit software power for profit, not malice, citing on‑screen store prompts.
events.title: Profit from user power

events.description: Stallman notes firms hold conferences to share tactics for exploiting users via proprietary software power.
events.title: Conferences on user exploitation

events.description: Stallman labels proprietary software as malware and calls it 'software for suckers'.
events.title: Software for suckers

events.description: Stallman invites listeners to join the free software movement instead of abandoning computers.
events.title: Join the free world

events.description: Stallman recalls his 1983 announcement to create a free operating system named GNU.
events.title: Announcing GNU OS

events.description: Richard Stallman explains that GNU was nearly complete in 1992, lacking only a kernel, which Linus Torvalds provided by releasing Linux, creating the first full GNU/Linux system.
events.title: GNU almost complete, Linux fills kernel

events.description: Stallman notes that GNU/Linux has over a thousand variants, known as distributions, and warns that freedom is not guaranteed.
events.title: Many GNU/Linux variants called distributions

events.description: Stallman says most GNU/Linux distributions include non‑free software for convenience, urging users to verify which distros are fully free.
events.title: Most distros add non‑free software for convenience

events.description: Stallman argues that preserving freedom may need sacrifices, citing Lexington as an example of a big sacrifice, but notes most are small and manageable.
events.title: Freedom requires small sacrifices

events.description: Stallman says wanting freedom may require giving up non‑free applications and accepting inconveniences.
events.title: To stay free, avoid non‑free applications

events.description: Stallman warns that websites send non‑free JavaScript to browsers and recommends installing LibreJS to block it.
events.title: Block non‑free JavaScript with LibreJS

events.description: Stallman describes how servers offer to compute your data in the cloud, hiding the process from users.
events.title: Cloud computing hides what servers do

events.description: Stallman urges users to examine cloud services, which act as software substitutes that relinquish computing control.
events.title: Service as a software substitute removes control

events.description: Richard Stallman argues that while many web servers run free software, personal computers should be freed first.
events.title: Stallman stresses freeing personal computers

events.description: Stallman says personal computers and people deserve freedom, calling for progress toward that goal.
events.title: Stallman calls for advancing user freedom

events.description: Stallman describes big companies profiting from user control as an obstacle to advancing free software.
events.title: Stallman identifies corporate control as obstacle

events.description: Stallman criticizes mainstream media for using "open source" to avoid discussing the ethical issues of free software.
events.title: Stallman critiques media's open source framing

events.description: Stallman contrasts free software activists' ethical stance with open source advocates' focus on practical improvements.
events.title: Stallman contrasts freedom vs. better quality

events.description: Stallman insists that preserving freedom requires discussing freedom itself, not just practical benefits.
events.title: Stallman urges talking about freedom

events.description: Stallman urges saying "free software" and criticizes schools teaching non‑free software as akin to encouraging tobacco use.
events.title: Stallman likens non‑free software to tobacco

events.description: Stallman argues schools should teach free software to foster independent, cooperative citizens in a free society.
events.title: Stallman advocates free software in schools

events.description: Stallman explains that studying free software lets students understand how it works, while nonfree software hides its knowledge, preventing learning.
events.title: Free vs nonfree software learning

events.description: He argues schools must use free software to uphold the spirit of education and hints at an even more important reason.
events.title: Education requires free software

events.description: Stallman says sharing programs in class should be like sharing cookies, requiring source code sharing so others can learn.
events.title: Sharing source code like cookies

events.description: He reiterates that sharing source code enables other people to learn from the program.
events.title: Share source code for learning

events.description: Stallman states students should bring only free software to class, except for reverse engineering, to set a good example.
events.title: Only free software in class

events.description: He notes manufacturers withhold hardware information, making it shocking that they sell products without telling users how to use them.
events.title: Hardware secrecy blocks free software

events.description: Stallman explains users must study binary code to understand hardware when manufacturers refuse to share usage details.
events.title: Reverse engineering hidden hardware

events.description: He urges examining binaries and documenting hardware so others can write free programs to operate it.
events.title: Document hardware for free software

events.description: Stallman says each new activity can bring new human rights that depend on each other, and losing one makes it harder to maintain the others.
events.title: Human rights interdependence

events.description: Stallman argues that because computing is important in society, the freedoms of free software are among the human rights that must be protected.
events.title: Free software as human right

events.description: Stallman states that society must establish and protect the freedoms of free software and asks how to help.
events.title: Protecting free software rights

events.description: Stallman lists actions: writing free software, organizing campaigns, persuading schools and governments to adopt free software, helping users install or use it, and spreading its philosophical ideas.
events.title: Ways to support free software

events.description: Stallman says moving to free software is the first step in liberating cyberspace, but also stresses the need for network neutrality and an end to general surveillance.
events.title: Free software and Internet freedoms

events.description: Applause is heard as Stallman finishes his point about software and Internet freedoms.
events.title: Audience applause

events.description: The screen shows text encouraging viewers to visit the TEDx website for more information.
events.title: TEDx info screen

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Free software is the first battle

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: in the liberation of cyberspace.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Who controls your computer?

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Is it you or is it some big company that's really controlling it?

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: What is a computer?

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: A computer is a universal machine.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: It will do any computation you want it to

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: because you give it a program that says

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: what the computation is that you want.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: The computer only knows how to get out an instruction and do it,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: and get out another instruction and do it.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: The program has the instructions, it says what to do.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: By writing the right program, you can make it do anything.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Well, almost anything.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Who gives the instructions to your computer?

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: You might think it's obeying your instructions

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: when really it's obeying somebody else first,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: and you only as much as that company will let it listen to you.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: With software, there are two possibilities:

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Either the users control the program, or the program controls the users.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: It's inevitably one or the other.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: In order for the users to control the program,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: they need the four essential freedoms.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: That's the definition of free software.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Free software respects the user's freedom and community.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Now, we often call it "Libre" using the French or Spanish word.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Pronounce it as you like, the point is that's what we mean.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: We don't mean it's gratis, we're not talking about price.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: We're concerned with your freedom,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: and we sometimes say "Free/Libre" to show that.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Freedom zero is the freedom to run the program

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: as you wish for whatever purpose.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Freedom one is the freedom to study the source code of the program

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: and change it, so it does the computing you want it to do.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: But what is the source code?

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Every program typically will have two forms.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: There's the form that you can read, and you can understand

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: if you know the programming language.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: That's the source.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: That's what programmers write and change.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Then, there's the executable, which is a bunch of numbers

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: which even a programmer can't figure out.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: If all you get is the executable,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: it's a horrible pain in the neck to the figure out what it does,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: and even harder to change it.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: So, to give you the real possibility to study and change it,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: they've got to give you the source code.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: That's a requirement.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: With those two freedoms,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: each user separately can make a copy

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: and start changing it and make it do what she wants.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: That's individual control.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: But what if you're not a programmer?

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: You look at the source code, and you don't understand it.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Individual control isn't enough.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: We also need collective control,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: which means any group of users are free to work together

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: to adapt the program to what they want.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Of course, in the group, some of them are programmers.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: They're the ones who actually write the changes,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: but they're doing it as part of the group

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: for what the group wants.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Of course, the group doesn't have to be everybody.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Others can use it some other way.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: They're all free to do that.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Collective control requires two more essential freedoms.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Freedom two is the freedom to redistribute exact copies,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: to make the copies and then give them away

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: or sell them when you wish.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Freedom three is similar,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: but it's for your modified versions.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: You're free to make copies, and then give them or sell them when you wish.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: If you do have these freedoms, then it's free software,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: the users control the program.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: But if any of those freedoms is missing,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: then the users don't control the program.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Instead, the program controls the users and the developer controls the program.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: So, that means this program is an instrument of unjust power

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: for its developer over the users.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: That means the users don't have freedom,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: that's non‑free, proprietary software which we've got to get rid of.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: When you've got proprietary software, what happens?

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Sometimes, the program snoops on the user.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Sometimes, it tracks the user.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Sometimes, it restricts the user,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: and stops users from doing what they want to do.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: You can see that the blue ray is your enemy.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: [Laughter]

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Sometimes, the software remotely deletes books

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: as Amazon did with "Nineteen Eighty-Four".

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Sometimes, the developer compels users

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: to install a harmful upgrade,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: by threatening to take away other functionality

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: if it's not installed, as Sony did.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Sometimes, they can even forcibly change the software at a distance

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: as Microsoft can with Windows through the universal back door.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Sometimes, they even sabotage users,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: as Microsoft does when it tells the NSA about bugs in Windows,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: so it can use them to attack people's computers.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: What you get is basically, with proprietary software,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: the owner has power over the users,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: and takes advantage of this power,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: putting in those various malicious functionalities

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: to hurt the users.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Of course, they don't do this because they're sadists;

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: they're doing it just for money, for greed.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: They have various ways that they can profit

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: from having this power over users,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: which does not make it even the tiniest bit less evil.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: But they have no shame about it.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: They have conferences where they talk about the latest ways

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: they can take advantage of users through the power they have.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Basically, proprietary software,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: which is now for almost all of the users of proprietary software,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: they're using proprietary malware.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: It's "software for suckers".

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: How do you stop being the victim?

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Formerly, you had to stop using computers, but not anymore.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Now, you can come join us in the free world that we've built.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: In 1983, I announced I would develop

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: a completely free software operating system called GNU.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: In 1992, we had it almost finished,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: but one piece was missing, the kernel.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Linus Torvalds, in that year, freed his kernel, Linux,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: which filled the last gap, and gave us

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: the first complete system you could run on a PC: GNU/Linux.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Unfortunately, having freedom at one point doesn't guarantee you'll keep it.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: There are over a thousand different variants of GNU/Linux.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: They're called distributions.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: A few of them are entirely free software;

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: most of them have non‑free software added,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: because they're maintained by people who aren't concerned about freedom.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: They'd rather add convenience -- but at the cost of freedom.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: So you have to check which is a free distro.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: To keep your freedom, sometimes requires a sacrifice,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: sometimes a big sacrifice, as at Lexington.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: But in our campaign, they tend to be little sacrifices.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Anybody with a little bit of maturity can make these sacrifices.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: For instance, you want applications, but some of them are non‑free.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: If you want freedom, you've got to do without them.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: There may be some inconveniences

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: you have to suffer for your freedom's sake.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Then, many websites send non‑free programs,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: written in JavaScript, to the user's browser.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: If you don't want to run non‑free programs,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: you should install LibreJS

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: which blocks, keeps out, non‑free JavaScript.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Sometimes, servers will offer to do your computing.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: They say, "Send us all your data."

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Obviously, for suckers.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Then the server does the computing, and sends you back the results.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: But you're not supposed to think about what's happening,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: because it's a "cloud", and you don't see what's going on.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Well, you should look.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: It's service as a software substitute,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: and it takes away control of your computing.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: A large fraction of the world's web servers

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: are running GNU/Linux and other free software.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: But I think the most important computers to put freedom in

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: are your computers, not companies' web servers.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: They deserve freedom, also.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: But above all, it's people that deserve freedom.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: So we need to advance,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: and to do that, we have to cross obstacles.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: One of them is there are big companies

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: that make a lot of money by having control over users.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: They don't want to let us advance.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: We have to overcome their opposition.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Another is that the mainstream media don't talk about free software.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: They have a term that they use to bury these ethical issues.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: They say "open source" instead.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Now, it talks about more or less the same programs,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: but with different ideas.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Where free software activists say,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: "This is a matter of right and wrong.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Users deserve freedom. We demand freedom."

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: The people who say open source, they don't want to say that.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Instead, they say,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: "Let the users change the software and redistribute it,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: and they'll make the code better.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: They'll fix some bugs."

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: It may be true, but it's a less important issue.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: If we want to keep our freedom, we've got to talk about freedom.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: So say, "free software," and you're helping us every time.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Another obstacle is that lots of schools teach non‑free software,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: which is basically like teaching the kids to smoke tobacco.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: It's implanting dependence,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: which is the opposite of what schools should do.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: A school should prepare citizens to live

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: in a strong, capable, independent, cooperating and free society,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: which means, teaching free software in the school.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: But there's another reason to do that for education.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Some kids want to become programmers, they're curious.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: They want to know how the programs work.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: While the one who's studying a free software can understand it,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: the one who's studying a non‑free program can't learn anything,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: because the knowledge in the non‑free program

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: is withheld, denied to the students.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: So to uphold the spirit of education,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: the school should make sure its programs are free.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: But there's an even more important reason:

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Schools should teach the spirit of goodwill,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: the habit of helping other people.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: The class should say,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: "If you bring a program to class,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: just as if you bring cookies to class,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: you've got to share it with everyone else.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: You can't keep it to yourself.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: You've got to share the source code, so other people can learn.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: So don't bring any proprietary software to this class."

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: The school has to set a good example by following its own rule:

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: You should bring only free software to class,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: except as a reverse engineering exercise.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Another obstacle is there's hardware

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: we don't know how to write free software for,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: because they won't tell us how to use the hardware.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: That's shocking. They want to sell you the product,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: and they won't tell you how to use it.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: They say, "Here's a non‑free program you can use.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: Run it, and shut up. Don't bother us."

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: How do we find out how to run that hardware with reverse engineering?

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: You've got to study all those 0's and 1's to figure out what they really do,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: and write down how to use that hardware,

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: so someone else can write the free program to do it.

transcript.speaker: speaker
transcript.text: It's hard work, but it can be done --
